title: Here Comes Treble

jokes.text: Michael... I mean Dwight's talking head opening: 'This year I decided to really get into the spirit of Halloween. It may have been the costliest decision I've ever made.'
jokes.setup: Dwight gravely announces he made 'the costliest decision of his life' — the phrasing implies financial or professional catastrophe.
jokes.punchline: The reveal is that he stuck his head in a pumpkin and can't get it out — a monumentally silly physical predicament framed with tragic gravitas.
jokes.explanation: The contrast between Dwight's overwrought gravitas and the absurd reality of the pumpkin head is pitch-perfect character comedy. Only Dwight would describe this as the 'costliest decision' of his life with complete sincerity. The misdirection structure is clean and the reveal earns its laugh. Strong but not exceptional — the joke is well-constructed but the concept (head stuck in pumpkin) is inherently broad.

jokes.text: Dwight with his head stuck in the pumpkin — Jim attempts to free him, and any blow to the pumpkin 'could prove fatal to me.'
jokes.setup: Dwight's head is literally stuck in a carved pumpkin. Jim is trying to help.
jokes.punchline: Dwight deadpans that any blow to the pumpkin 'could prove fatal to me' — treating the situation with the seriousness of a hostage crisis.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Dwight speaking calmly with a pumpkin on his head while assessing mortal danger is strong character comedy. 'Prove fatal to me' is a great line — clinical, detached, and completely Dwight. The visual gag also gives the talking head format a wonderful absurdist twist since we're presumably seeing him post-incident narrating this.

jokes.text: 'At first I drove myself crazy thinking about what I should've done differently... But then I realized I was being silly. I mean, the pumpkin should rot off of my head in a month or two.'
jokes.setup: Dwight describes regretting his choices, leading the audience to expect a normal resolution.
jokes.punchline: His solution is simply to wait for the pumpkin to biologically decompose off his head — delivered with complete calm rationality.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the cold open and arguably the episode. The structure is masterful: Dwight performs genuine self-reflection, appears to arrive at wisdom, then delivers the most insane possible 'rational' conclusion with zero irony. The word 'rot' is doing enormous comedic work — it's visceral, it's specific, it's perfect. Only Dwight Schrute would both (a) get his head stuck in a pumpkin and (b) decide the best course of action is patient decomposition. This approaches the upper tier of The Office's joke writing. The beat pause after 'in a month or two' followed by 'Right?' seals it.

jokes.text: Dwight's uncertain 'Right?' at the end of the cold open — a rare crack in his confidence, looking to the camera for reassurance.
jokes.setup: Dwight has just confidently announced the pumpkin will rot off his head as if this is a perfectly reasonable plan.
jokes.punchline: The tiny word 'Right?' reveals genuine uncertainty — he's actually not sure this will work and needs validation from the documentary crew.
jokes.explanation: A single word delivering a massive comedic payload. The 'Right?' punctures Dwight's unearned confidence perfectly and rewards attentive viewers. It's the best kind of economy: maximum character revelation in minimum words. The callback structure (delivered immediately after joke 3) means it functions as both a topper and a character beat. Very hard to pull off.

jokes.text: Pam's costume: 'I'm Dr. Cinderella. Cece's really into princesses now, so we decided to turn them into positive female role models. I'm an oncologist.'
jokes.setup: Pam reveals her Halloween costume is 'Dr. Cinderella.'
jokes.punchline: The explanation — making Disney princesses into positive female role models — culminates in 'I'm an oncologist,' which is simultaneously admirable, earnest, and absurd as a Halloween costume.
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational joke about millennial parenting anxiety filtered through Pam's specific character. The word 'oncologist' is the perfectly wrong choice — it's a real career, technically positive, but a deeply unsexy Halloween costume for a child's princess story. The joke has Pam's earnest energy all over it. Well-constructed.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I am one of the Men in Black guys.' Pam: 'Can I have your sunglasses?' Jim: 'Jim, come on. I thought we were past this.'
jokes.setup: Jim claims he IS dressed up — as a Man in Black. He's clearly just wearing his normal work clothes.
jokes.punchline: Pam's 'Can I have your sunglasses?' exposes that he has no costume props either. Jim's self-aware 'I thought we were past this' acknowledges his own lazy annual ritual.
jokes.explanation: A reliable running gag for the series (Jim's non-costumes) that works because of character specificity. Pam's 'Can I have your sunglasses?' is a clean expose of the costume's poverty. The exchange is comfortable, well-timed, but not particularly inventive — it's the show coasting on established character dynamics.

jokes.text: Pam talking head about Jim's sports marketing business: 'So the sports marketing business that Jim told everyone about except for me... There's a big investment lunch today... Unless he has a secret costume that he told everyone about except for me.'
jokes.setup: Pam explains the serious situation — Jim has been excluding her from his business plans.
jokes.punchline: She pivots the marital resentment into a wry joke about the costume, landing the bitterness with a comedic sting rather than melodrama.
jokes.explanation: The structure is clever — Pam uses the talking-head format to layer the joke with real emotional stakes, making the comedic pivot land harder. The repetition of 'except for me' is a well-deployed device that builds rhythm. Functions as both character development and comedy, which is the show at its best.

jokes.text: Jim to Pam: 'Getting a lot of mileage out of this, aren't you?' Pam: 'Yeah, well, get used to it, bud.'
jokes.setup: Jim realizes Pam is going to keep working the 'he didn't tell me' angle.
jokes.punchline: 'Get used to it, bud' — cheerful, direct, and slightly threatening. The word 'bud' does a lot of work.
jokes.explanation: Solid marital banter. The line 'Get used to it, bud' has the right cadence and the affectionate-threatening energy of a long-term relationship's passive aggression. 'Bud' is the killer word — too friendly for a genuine fight, too pointed to be wholly warm.

jokes.text: Kevin's costume: 'Jitterbug'
jokes.setup: Kevin appears at the party. His costume is referenced verbally.
jokes.punchline: Kevin is dressed as a 'Jitterbug' — the phone marketed to senior citizens. The audience presumably sees a large man dressed as a chunky flip phone designed for old people.
jokes.explanation: The joke functions almost entirely as a visual gag — Kevin as a Jitterbug (elderly-person phone) has layers of comedy: the sheer randommness of the choice, the fact that Kevin probably picked it earnestly, and the implicit commentary that Kevin relates to something designed for confused elderly people. Works better on screen than on page.

jokes.text: Angela: 'The Senator will be joining us later.' Dwight: 'Not a question.' Angela: 'No, it wasn't.' Andy: 'Excellent.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks for questions after a party announcement.
jokes.punchline: Angela inserts an announcement about the Senator — not a question. Dwight's 'Not a question' call-out and the subsequent straight acknowledgments create a dry comedic exchange about social awkwardness.
jokes.explanation: A neat little three-beat exchange that plays on meeting-room protocol awkwardness. Dwight's pedantic correction is in character, and Angela's unflappable 'No, it wasn't' is perfect. Competent but unremarkable — functions as setup for the Senator subplot.

jokes.text: Andy reveals Here Comes Treble was hiding in the office, bursting in to perform 'Karma Chameleon'
jokes.setup: Andy has been asking cryptically if anyone has 'seen any treble' — setting up a groan-worthy pun.
jokes.punchline: A full Cornell a cappella group storms the office performing 'Karma Chameleon' as Andy watches with maximum self-satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: The 'seen any treble' pun is groan-worthy but the escalation into a full a cappella ambush is genuinely funny. The joke is really about Andy's desperate need to be cool in front of his Cornell connections and coworkers simultaneously. The performance itself is the punchline — the enthusiasm versus the uncomfortable audience reaction tells the whole story.

jokes.text: After Treble performs: 'What lab did these little clones escape from?' / 'My Cornell a cappella group.' / 'You went to Cornell?'
jokes.setup: Dwight mockingly asks what lab produced the identical-looking a cappella boys.
jokes.punchline: The successive reveals — Andy was in an a cappella group, and Andy went to Cornell — each get their own beat of mock-surprise, with 'You went to Cornell?' landing as the bigger punchline.
jokes.explanation: The two-beat reveal structure is well-constructed. 'What lab did these little clones escape from?' is a fun Dwight line. The comedy of 'You went to Cornell?' is that it treats this as the more shocking of the two revelations — and for a character as Andy comes across, maybe it is. Efficient and fun.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'Ugh, I don't want to sit through a whole concert of that.' Clark: 'I do! I love the boss' interests!' Andy: 'Attaboy, Clark.'
jokes.setup: The group discusses the upcoming a cappella set.
jokes.punchline: Clark's shameless sycophancy ('I love the boss' interests!') is called out and rewarded simultaneously — Andy, oblivious, takes it as genuine.
jokes.explanation: A solid three-person exchange demonstrating Andy's blind vanity and Clark's strategic brown-nosing. 'Attaboy, Clark' is perfect Andy — condescending, oblivious, exactly what Clark wanted. The joke works because the audience sees all three layers Andy cannot.

jokes.text: Andy to the Treble members: 'Where you boys staying? How does it work in the rooms? You get a privacy partition?'
jokes.setup: Andy is attempting to bond with the young a cappella members as a respected elder.
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks intrusive questions about their sleeping arrangements — the question reveals both his nosiness and his misguided attempt at insider camaraderie.
jokes.explanation: Mild cringe comedy that establishes Andy's social obliviousness. The 'privacy partition' question is a bit odd but not laugh-out-loud funny — it works better as texture for the episode's Andy arc than as a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Andy talking head: 'They might actually call me up to solo on George Michael's Faith. That was one of my signature songs. Oh man. That would be insane. I'm so not prepared.'
jokes.setup: Andy fantasizes about being invited to solo at the office party.
jokes.punchline: His excitement collapses immediately into panic — 'I'm so not prepared' — revealing he's already cast himself as the star of a performance he wasn't invited to.
jokes.explanation: The rapid self-inflation and deflation is very Andy. 'That was one of my signature songs' followed immediately by 'I'm so not prepared' creates a mini-arc of delusion and insecurity in three seconds. Good character writing that also plants the Faith payoff.

jokes.text: Dwight eating Nerds candy shaped like Jim's head: 'Jim, look, I'm eating you.' / 'Must eat more Jims!'
jokes.setup: Dwight has obtained Nerds candy that apparently resemble Jim (or he's labeled them as such).
jokes.punchline: Dwight and then Erin dramatize eating Jim — Dwight with smug satisfaction, Erin with monster-movie energy — while Jim grows increasingly annoyed.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels — Dwight's glee at symbolically consuming Jim is peak rivalry energy, and Erin's enthusiastic participation ('Must eat more Jims!') escalates it into something genuinely silly. Jim's 'Shut up' and his increasing agitation ('Stop it! Stop it!') as candy spills is good physical comedy. The pumpkin-head context makes Jim's fury funnier since he's already having a bad day.

jokes.text: Jim screaming 'Stop it! Stop it! Stop it! Stop it! Stop it!' as Nerds candy spills everywhere
jokes.setup: The eating-Jim candy gag has escalated with Erin joining in.
jokes.punchline: Jim's completely disproportionate five-fold 'Stop it!' as candy cascades is a funny crack in his usual cool — the unflappable straight man utterly flapped.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Jim's response from one 'shut up' to five consecutive 'Stop its' is a well-timed comedic escalation. Jim losing his composure is always funny because it's so rare. The physical comedy of spilling candy adds to it.

jokes.text: Dwight finds a pill and interrogates it: 'Hello, little pill. What do you do?' Then reads the label like a diagnosis: 'There's a madman in our midst.'
jokes.setup: Dwight finds a pill on the floor and treats it like a crime scene artifact.
jokes.punchline: 'There's a madman in our midst' — Dwight's theatrical conclusion from a found anxiety pill. He's treating an extremely common medication as evidence of violent psychosis.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight — maximum paranoia, minimum information. 'Hello, little pill' is a disarmingly gentle opening that makes the jump to 'madman in our midst' all the funnier. The joke is about Dwight's complete inability to contextualize mental health medication as normal. High character integration; this scene couldn't work with any other character.

jokes.text: Toby appears in costume: 'I'm Sexy Toby.' Oscar: 'Gross! I love it.'
jokes.setup: Toby reveals his Halloween costume.
jokes.punchline: The concept of 'Sexy Toby' — Toby, the most desexualized character in the show — dressed provocatively. Oscar's 'Gross! I love it!' captures the audience's reaction perfectly.
jokes.explanation: The joke is almost entirely in the concept — Toby as 'Sexy Toby' is funny because Toby is constitutionally incapable of being sexy. The character is defined by his listlessness and sadness. Oscar's two-word reaction ('Gross! I love it!') is the perfect articulation of the audience's conflicted delight. The visual gag we're meant to infer (Toby in some kind of revealing/seductive getup) sells it.

jokes.text: Dwight's escalating taxonomy of the pill: 'This is a pill for a disorder of the mind.' / 'It combats insanity.' / 'Whoever is taking it is not only insane, they are now off their meds.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been analyzing the found anxiety pill and building his case.
jokes.punchline: The three-step escalation from 'disorder of the mind' to 'insanity' to 'now off their meds' — each step more dramatically wrong than the last.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is well-built. Each beat lands a separate mini-laugh as Dwight's conclusions become more extreme. 'Not only insane, they are NOW OFF THEIR MEDS' is delivered with the urgency of a public health emergency. Dwight's certainty makes the comedy work — he's not performing alarm, he IS alarmed.

jokes.text: Nellie: 'I once saw him yell at Phyllis for sneezing wrong.'
jokes.setup: Nellie explains why she doesn't want Dwight knowing about her anxiety medication.
jokes.punchline: The specific, absurd detail — Dwight yelling at someone for 'sneezing wrong' — serves as devastating shorthand for Dwight's irrationality.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines. The specificity of 'sneezing wrong' is inspired — it implies Dwight has a correct way to sneeze that he's codified and enforces. It's economical (five words doing enormous character work), instantly quotable, and perfectly captures Dwight's controlling nature without him being present. The line works as both a joke about Dwight AND as character work for Nellie.

jokes.text: 'Okay, this is a pill that combats insanity. Whoever is taking it is not only insane, they are now off their meds.'
jokes.setup: Dwight builds his case about the pill
jokes.punchline: His logic is internally consistent but completely wrong in every direction — and his concern is framed as civic duty rather than compassion
jokes.explanation: The cold logic of 'not only insane, but now off their meds' is a nice escalation. Dwight's entire pill subplot is consistent world-building for his character. Solid.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Yeah, you're right. This man needs to be apprehended. I'll get my apprehension kit.'
jokes.setup: Toby suggests that whoever has anxiety needs help, not suspicion.
jokes.punchline: Dwight agrees ('you're right') but completely misunderstands the lesson — his solution is to apprehend the 'dangerous' person with a dedicated kit.
jokes.explanation: The structure is brilliant: Dwight appears to be capitulating to reason ('yeah, you're right') before revealing he's arrived at an even more extreme response. The existence of an 'apprehension kit' — casually mentioned as if it's normal office equipment — is perfect Dwight worldbuilding. The line lands hard because of the pivot structure and the casual specificity of 'apprehension kit.'

jokes.text: Andy talking head: 'When I got the nickname Boner Champ, that is when I became me.'
jokes.setup: Andy is reflecting on his identity-forming experiences at Cornell with Here Comes Treble.
jokes.punchline: The nickname 'Boner Champ' is delivered with complete sincerity as the moment Andy found himself — treating an objectively absurd title as a genuine coming-of-age revelation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure — building genuine emotional sincerity ('that is when I became me') around the nickname 'Boner Champ' — is a masterclass in comedic deflation. The line works because Andy means it completely. The camera slowly holding on his earnest face after this statement is the kind of mockumentary comic timing the show excels at. Quotable, character-perfect, and the foundation of the episode's best running gag.

jokes.text: Andy: 'You got Q's, I got A's.' / Treble member: 'Did you say you've got AIDS?' / Andy: 'No, I don't have AIDS. That's not what I said. Next question.'
jokes.setup: Andy invites questions from the young a cappella group using the slang abbreviation 'Q's' and 'A's.'
jokes.punchline: The abbreviation 'A's' is misheard as 'AIDS' — a mondegreen that Andy must deny before moving on as if this is perfectly normal.
jokes.explanation: The AIDS misunderstanding is a well-executed wordplay joke. The comedy is in Andy's brisk 'No, I don't have AIDS. That's not what I said. Next question.' — he moves past it with the efficiency of someone who's used to managing embarrassing misunderstandings. The 'Next question' is the kicker that sells it. Somewhat cheap conceptually (shock word for laugh) but well-executed.

jokes.text: Andy: 'You at least want to know why they call me Boner Champ?' / Treble member: 'I thought Broccoli Rob was the Boner Champ.'
jokes.setup: Andy, clearly desperate for the young members' validation, offers to explain his legendary nickname.
jokes.punchline: The member casually reveals that everyone thinks Broccoli Rob is the Boner Champ — the title Andy considers his core identity has been misattributed.
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Boner Champ' combined with the complete deflation of Andy's identity is beautifully structured. 'I thought Broccoli Rob was the Boner Champ' hits on multiple levels: (1) the name 'Broccoli Rob' is funny on its own, (2) the casual delivery suggests everyone has always thought this, (3) it destroys Andy's self-conception in one sentence. The pauses between Andy's repetitions of the claim in his talking head ('Broccoli Rob was Broccoli Rob. Andy Bernard is the Boner Champ.') are devastating mockumentary comedy.

jokes.text: Andy talking head: 'Broccoli Rob was Broccoli Rob.' [long pause] 'Andy Bernard is the Boner Champ.'
jokes.setup: Andy is reeling from the revelation that people think Broccoli Rob is the Boner Champ.
jokes.punchline: He makes the distinction with the gravity of a man correcting a historical record — the pauses between statements carrying enormous weight.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The structure is perfect: two declarative sentences separated by a beat, each delivered with the seriousness of a congressional testimony. 'Broccoli Rob was Broccoli Rob' functions as its own absurdist statement (tautological, solemn, oddly profound). The follow-up 'Andy Bernard is the Boner Champ' is Andy's entire identity compressed into a sentence he delivers like a Supreme Court ruling. The economy is extraordinary — ten words doing the emotional work of a monologue. Ed Helms' performance makes this transcendent. Comparable to 'Snip, snap' in terms of character-driven comedic escalation delivered through absolute sincerity.

jokes.text: Ryan and Kelly both appearing without costumes — 'I didn't realize that everybody here dresses up every year.' 'Me neither.' 'It's Halloween.'
jokes.setup: Two characters appear in regular clothes amidst a costumed office.
jokes.punchline: Their mutual ignorance of a recurring annual event on one of the most recognizable holidays is treated as a reasonable position.
jokes.explanation: A mild joke that functions more as a background gag. It's mildly funny that two people don't know their own office dresses up for Halloween, but the joke lacks edge. The payoff is just the obvious statement 'It's Halloween,' which is the straightest of straight man lines.

jokes.text: Andy to Broccoli Rob on the phone: begging him to set the Boner Champ record straight — Rob apparently did it 'and I guess the wine coolers were flowing, and you know, somehow things just got hinky.'
jokes.setup: Andy has discovered his identity has been misappropriated and calls Broccoli Rob to fix it.
jokes.punchline: Rob's explanation — wine coolers were flowing and 'things got hinky' — is both the most and least helpful thing he could say, explaining nothing while Andy's desperation grows.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'things got hinky' is a great period-appropriate euphemism that reveals the utter absurdity of the whole situation. The cringe comes from witnessing Andy beg someone to confirm his college nickname — and having to rely on another person entirely to rehabilitate his own reputation.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'Hey, Darryl. I'm just here to smear some peanut butter on my forehead. You know, to protect his brain from the nanobots that the government put in the air conditioning.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is apparently testing Darryl to see if he'll accept an insane premise (part of his hunt for the anxiety-pill owner).
jokes.punchline: The nanobots-in-the-air-conditioning conspiracy theory combined with peanut butter as protective gear is a gloriously specific piece of Dwight absurdism.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'nanobots' and the domestic mundaneness of 'peanut butter' is a great comedic pairing. Dwight's sanity-test has the internal logic of a Dwight Schrute operation — completely insane from outside, rigorously structured from within. The visual of Dwight smearing peanut butter on his own forehead (with a pumpkin on his head) is probably outstanding.

jokes.text: Darryl egging Dwight on: 'Maybe get the cheeks.' / 'Is that where the nanobots like to come in?' / 'Get all the way up to your lip, yeah.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is performing his peanut butter nanobot test on Darryl, expecting Darryl to protest.
jokes.punchline: Darryl instead leans into it with complete deadpan sincerity, directing Dwight to apply more peanut butter, treating the insane premise as entirely reasonable — until the reveal that 'Yeah, that's crazy.'
jokes.explanation: Darryl's deadpan cooperation escalating to 'get under your chin' followed by the flat 'yeah, that's crazy' is a wonderfully structured bit. The joke is in Darryl playing along with complete commitment before calmly pulling the rug. The reversal — Dwight was testing Darryl, Darryl ends up testing Dwight — is smart. Darryl's straight-man work here is excellent.

jokes.text: Andy explains how he got the name Boner Champ: 'Spring Sing '95, we got completely ripped on Bud Drys, I had sex with a snowman. I just went at that thing. The cold would've stopped most people, but I stayed locked in... I took the face off. Just seemed easier that way.'
jokes.setup: The young Treble members and/or others ask Andy how he earned the Boner Champ title.
jokes.punchline: The escalating details — Bud Dry, a snowman, removing the face for efficiency — build to a genuinely shocking and absurd explanation delivered with the casual pride of a war hero recounting a battle.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak alongside joke 26. The story has everything: a specific, perfectly evocative detail (Bud Drys, Spring Sing '95), escalating absurdity (a snowman), the practical problem-solving detail ('I took the face off — just seemed easier that way'), and Andy's complete earnestness throughout. The line 'The cold would've stopped most people, but I stayed locked in' is the engine of the joke — it reframes the act as one requiring dedication and resilience. Only Andy Bernard could tell this story with zero self-awareness and complete pride. This is the kind of joke that defines a character and gets quoted for years.

jokes.text: 'And I told Phyllis not to put it out, but she insisted. So, anyway, hi.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just finished describing in detail his sexual encounter with a snowman
jokes.punchline: He references Phyllis having put out the very snowman he desecrated (at the party they're now attending) — then the whiplash transition to 'So, anyway, hi' as he greets Oscar and the Senator
jokes.explanation: The best structural joke in the episode. Andy's snowman sex story has been delivered as a confessional, but 'I told Phyllis not to put it out' snaps it into the present — that snowman is HERE, at this party. The pivot to 'So, anyway, hi' — the most casual possible greeting after this revelation — is perfect timing and perfect character voice. It simultaneously closes the snowman bit and opens the Senator/Oscar awkward encounter. Exceptional economy and structure.

jokes.text: Senator Lipton: 'Wait a second. Who designed this spread? The sweets and savories are all mixed together. This is mayhem.' Then immediately abandons Oscar to find Phyllis.
jokes.setup: Angela introduces the Senator to Oscar at the Halloween party. This is loaded with the dramatic irony that the Senator is secretly having an affair with Oscar.
jokes.punchline: The Senator immediately becomes distracted by the buffet layout and runs off, leaving Oscar and Angela together — with 'God, it's just so good to see you' delivered with completely misplaced warmth.
jokes.explanation: The joke operates on two levels: the Senator's absurd priorities (buffet layout as 'mayhem') and the dramatic irony of Angela cheerfully throwing Oscar and the Senator together. 'God, it's just so good to see you' is funnier knowing what we know. The escape via buffet complaint is a nicely specific comic detail.

jokes.text: Andy to Here Comes Treble: 'You all go to Cornell. You're, like, eight Rain Men. Just learn the fricking song.'
jokes.setup: Andy is demanding the group learn 'Faith' in time for the party concert.
jokes.punchline: 'You're like eight Rain Men' — Andy's compliment-as-insult demand, invoking Rain Man as a compliment to Cornell students while also revealing his completely distorted view of intellectual capacity.
jokes.explanation: The 'eight Rain Men' line is punchy and reveals Andy's paradoxical relationship with intelligence — he thinks Cornell = Rain Man, which is simultaneously complimentary and offensive. The specific number 'eight' makes it funnier. Andy's desperation makes the demand land harder.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Look, I know it was big with the old guys, but...' / Russell: 'Butts are for pooping.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to have a serious conversation about the feasibility of learning 'Faith.'
jokes.punchline: Russell interrupts with 'Butts are for pooping' — a complete non-sequitur that suggests either immaturity or an established a cappella in-joke. Either way, it's perfectly timed.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the absolute precision of the interruption — 'but...' leaves a gap that 'Butts are for pooping' fills with devastating literalism. It's absurdist and juvenile in equal measure, and the fact that it's delivered by a young Ivy League a cappella singer makes it funnier. The economy is perfect: four words, maximum disruption.

jokes.text: Beat following the Toby/Toby costume reveal — two Tobys staring at each other
jokes.setup: Toby (Sexy Toby) encounters someone dressed as Toby.
jokes.punchline: The long silent beat of mutual recognition — two Tobys contemplating each other — is the joke. The uncomfortable pause carries the existential weight of Toby's entire character.
jokes.explanation: The Toby-as-Toby costume reveal is a wonderfully bleak joke. The visual of Toby confronting another Toby (who dressed as 'Toby Flenderson' for Halloween — already a sad choice) while he himself is 'Sexy Toby' creates layers of comedic pathos. The silence does all the work. 'It's funny, right?' is the final puncture — Toby needing confirmation that even his own meta-costume lands.

jokes.text: 'This isn't stupid.' — delivered into space after Andy exits, apparently to himself
jokes.setup: Andy has just given an extremely emotional and slightly unhinged speech about 'Faith' being his signature song
jokes.punchline: He pauses alone and quietly insists to himself — or the documentary camera — 'This isn't stupid,' which of course confirms that it is, and that he knows it
jokes.explanation: Three words delivering an entire emotional arc. Andy saying 'This isn't stupid' alone after a sequence that was objectively stupid, with the camera presumably on him, is a masterclass in Office-style confessional comedy. The fact that he says it quietly, possibly to himself, rather than to the camera makes it more devastating. Character integration is near-perfect — this is Andy's core vulnerability. The silence/pause before and after amplifies it.

jokes.text: Two Tobys: 'Look at me.' / 'Being you.' / 'I know! Look at you.' / 'It's funny, right?'
jokes.setup: Two people dressed as Toby are having the most pathetic possible encounter.
jokes.punchline: 'It's funny, right?' — Toby needs explicit confirmation from another version of himself that the joke lands. The existential sadness and the comedy are inseparable.
jokes.explanation: 'It's funny, right?' is the perfect Toby line — needy, self-aware, and ultimately unanswered. The meta-comedy of someone dressed as Toby asking Toby if it's funny collapses the joke and the character into the same moment. This is high-craft character work; only Toby Flenderson's existence could produce this.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'You think I don't have anxiety? I have anxiety all the time! Every waking moment of my life is sheer torture! I have land disputes to settle, and idiot cousins to protect, and ne'er-do-well siblings to take care of.'
jokes.setup: Toby suggests that anxiety is common and Dwight should drop his investigation.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's defense of his own non-pill-taking mental health reveals that his life is objectively more stressful and chaotic than anyone's — the specificity of 'land disputes' and 'ne'er-do-well siblings' is delightful.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character comedy moments. The joke is that Dwight's list of stressors — intended to prove he doesn't need anxiety medication — inadvertently demonstrates that he absolutely does. 'Land disputes,' 'idiot cousins,' 'ne'er-do-well siblings' are all simultaneously funny and completely in-universe for Dwight. The phrase 'every waking moment of my life is sheer torture' delivered as a point of pride is extraordinary character writing. The line 'ne'er-do-well siblings' in particular has a Dickensian quality that perfectly captures Dwight's anachronistic self-image.

jokes.text: Dwight nets Nellie with his 'apprehension kit' — apparently a literal net — while Nellie tries to reason with him
jokes.setup: Dwight promised to retrieve his apprehension kit
jokes.punchline: He actually does — and uses a net to physically capture Nellie, who is yelling 'Don't dog catch me!'
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff of the apprehension kit is fully earned and funnier for having been set up. The kit apparently contains a net — suggesting Dwight's preparedness is both literal and unhinged. 'Don't dog catch me!' from Nellie is a great spontaneous line. Solid physical escalation.

jokes.text: Dwight chases Meredith with a net; chaos ensues with Dwight yelling 'The jig is up, Psychopath!'
jokes.setup: Meredith grabs the anxiety pill; Dwight's apprehension kit apparently includes a net
jokes.punchline: Dwight tackles Meredith with his apprehension kit while yelling 'The jig is up, Psychopath!' — the net is the payoff to 'I'll get my apprehension kit'
jokes.explanation: The payoff to 'I'll get my apprehension kit' is the best possible version of that joke — Dwight actually has a net, and he uses it. 'The jig is up, Psychopath!' directed at Meredith for taking an anxiety pill is unhinged. The physical chaos of a pumpkin-headed man with a net is visually absurd. Strong escalation payoff.

jokes.text: Nellie drops a net/apprehension on the chase scene — 'Let's see you get out of this web.' / 'The pill is mine!'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been hunting the pill's owner, Nellie has been trying to retrieve it.
jokes.punchline: The confrontation devolves into a physical struggle over an anxiety pill — Dwight with his apprehension kit, Nellie fighting back — culminating in 'Stop banging my head!' (the pumpkin on Dwight's head being jostled).
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of Dwight and Nellie wrestling over an anxiety pill is good broad comedy, made better by the pumpkin-head detail returning. 'The pill is mine!' is a gloriously petty battle cry. The scene pays off the apprehension kit setup from earlier. Broad but earned.

jokes.text: Nellie confesses it's her pill: 'I take it every day, and it makes me feel better. And maybe it could help you too.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has captured Nellie believing he's found the 'psychopath'
jokes.punchline: Nellie's calm admission — followed by the suggestion that Dwight might also benefit — is both the resolution of the subplot and a nice character moment; the joke is the gentle offer to Dwight
jokes.explanation: The comic irony of Nellie suggesting Dwight might benefit from anti-anxiety medication — after he's just spent the episode in a manic investigation culminating in netting a coworker — lands as a quiet, satisfying button to the subplot. Not a big laugh but well-earned.

jokes.text: Pam and Jim post-investment reveal: Jim dodging how much he invested ('About 10') / Pam: 'About 10? Ten. It was the full 10.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to confess he invested $10,000 without telling Pam.
jokes.punchline: His hedge ('about 10') is immediately punctured by his own clarification ('it was the full 10') — the self-own of someone who talked himself into a corner.
jokes.explanation: The cringe comedy of Jim's attempted softening ('about 10') being immediately cancelled by his own words is well-structured. Pam's flat 'About 10? Ten. It was the full 10.' is the kind of line that plays perfectly in the context of a real marriage argument — she's not yelling, she's just making him say it clearly.

jokes.text: Jim: 'You know, it's a good thing we talked about it, though' / Pam's incredulous beat / Jim: 'Because we had to. Yeah, yeah. I know.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to spin the situation positively — 'It's a good thing we talked about it.'
jokes.punchline: The implication that talking about it was his plan all along collapses under Pam's wordless response, forcing Jim to immediately retreat.
jokes.explanation: Jim's conversational gymnastics are recognizably human — the attempt to retroactively present the fight as productive, followed by immediate capitulation. Pam's reaction beat (the pause before he gives up) is where the comedy lives. Good use of the mockumentary format's silent reaction.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam arguing over the $10,000 investment while Here Comes Treble performs in the background — 'No, I want to talk about it now!' over soft a cappella
jokes.setup: The concert is happening. Jim and Pam are having a genuine marital argument about money.
jokes.punchline: The absurd juxtaposition of a tender a cappella performance providing soundtrack to a tense money fight. The more sincere the music, the funnier the argument.
jokes.explanation: Classic Office tonal juxtaposition — emotionally loaded marital conflict underscored by earnest a cappella singing. The music makes the argument funnier and the argument makes the music more awkward. A technique the show does well.

jokes.text: After the a cappella performance, the group does car wash sounds — 'Get your car washed today' / 'Ba-da-bah' / etc. Andy: 'That's how you do that!'
jokes.setup: Here Comes Treble has been performing earnest a cappella. They pivot to a car wash jingle.
jokes.punchline: Andy's unbridled enthusiasm ('That's how you do that!') for an objectively cornball car wash jingle reveals the depth of his a cappella fandom.
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny — the car wash jingle performed with a cappella earnestness is inherently comic, and Andy's ecstatic response contrasts with the crowd's implied indifference. The joke works more as a scene beat than a standalone comedy moment.

jokes.text: Treble begins 'Faith'... and Broccoli Rob walks in to sing it
jokes.setup: Andy has been desperate to perform 'Faith' — his signature song. The group was asked to prepare it for him.
jokes.punchline: Broccoli Rob, the man who stole Andy's Boner Champ identity, appears to sing Andy's signature song at Andy's office party — the ultimate indignity.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the episode's central Andy plot is beautifully structured. Every element has been planted: Faith as signature song, Broccoli Rob's identity theft, Andy's desperate desire for recognition. Having all three collide in one moment — at Andy's own workplace, announced to his staff — is excellent long-game comedy writing. The structure is almost operatic in how it brings Andy's humiliation to its nadir.

jokes.text: Andy: 'What the hell is Broccoli Rob doing here?' / Erin: 'She said you wanted to hear Faith.' / Andy: 'That's Broccoli Rob's signature song... That's MY signature song.' / Russell: 'I thought you were Adam Lambert.'
jokes.setup: Broccoli Rob has appeared to sing Faith at Andy's office party.
jokes.punchline: Russell's 'I thought you were Adam Lambert' — mistaking Andy's George Michael costume for Adam Lambert — piles on the indignity. Andy's own costume identity has been misread, mirroring his Boner Champ erasure.
jokes.explanation: The Adam Lambert confusion is a beautifully placed additional knife — Andy dressed as George Michael to signal his connection to 'Faith,' but his costume itself has been misidentified. It's a thematic echo of the Boner Champ misattribution: Andy's identity, again, is being assigned to someone else. Smart construction.

jokes.text: 'I thought you were Adam Lambert.' — Russell's defense when Andy says he dressed as George Michael
jokes.setup: Andy is furious that Broccoli Rob is singing his signature song; Russell explains that he didn't know Andy wanted to sing it
jokes.punchline: 'I thought you were Adam Lambert' — Russell genuinely misidentified Andy's George Michael costume, which is both an insult and an explanation
jokes.explanation: The specific choice of Adam Lambert as the misidentification is excellent — he's a valid connection (same era, same gay icon territory, similar look) but crucially NOT George Michael, which invalidates Andy's entire costume premise. Specific, efficient, funny.

jokes.text: Oscar talking head about Angela/Senator: 'The more I hear about all this a cappella drama, the more I think it's kind of pathetic. But when you're with someone, you put up with the stuff that makes you lose respect for them, and that is love.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is nominally commenting on Andy's a cappella drama.
jokes.punchline: The speech is transparently about Oscar's own situation with the Senator — putting up with someone whose behavior makes you lose respect for them. Oscar is describing being the Senator's secret affair, framed as relationship wisdom.
jokes.explanation: The double-meaning talking head is a sophisticated piece of comedy writing. On the surface, it's Oscar being snobbish about a cappella. Underneath, it's a painful self-description of his situation with a married closeted senator. 'That is love' lands with genuine pathos and dark irony simultaneously. The Office at its best layers comedy with character revelation.

jokes.text: Broccoli Rob explaining himself: 'Russell called me up, and they said they needed 20 cc's of George Michael, stat. So, just wham! I sprang into action. You know me.'
jokes.setup: Broccoli Rob is defending his appearance at Andy's party to sing Faith.
jokes.punchline: '20 cc's of George Michael, stat' — a medical emergency framing for an a cappella request, delivered with complete self-satisfied casualness ('You know me').
jokes.explanation: One of the best one-liners in the episode. '20 cc's of George Michael, stat' is a perfectly constructed absurdist line that works on multiple levels: the medical urgency framing, the specific unit of measurement ('cc's'), the specific artist name, and the self-satisfied 'You know me' that suggests Broccoli Rob has a heroic self-image. The line is instantly quotable and funny in isolation.

jokes.text: Andy: 'You thought I wanted to sit in the audience like some slutty Treb rat?' / Broccoli Rob: 'A man's signature solo is his for life, okay? That's group policy, and you know it.'
jokes.setup: Andy is outraged at Broccoli Rob performing 'his' song.
jokes.punchline: 'A man's signature solo is his for life. That's group policy' — Andy invoking formal a cappella group bylaws about solo ownership, as if this is a legal dispute.
jokes.explanation: 'Slutty Treb rat' is a great piece of invented a cappella slang. 'Group policy' being invoked for solo ownership rights is funny because it treats the a cappella world as having serious institutional structure — which, for people like Andy and Broccoli Rob, it clearly does. The argument has the genuine heat of a real grievance, which makes the absurdity more funny.

jokes.text: Broccoli Rob: 'It's not my fault I still live near campus. And it's my duty as an alum to be friendly to the young guys, and stop in two, three times a week.'
jokes.setup: Broccoli Rob is defending why he's still so involved with a college a cappella group as a full adult.
jokes.punchline: 'Two, three times a week' — the revelation that a grown adult attends college a cappella practice several times a week 'as his duty' is grimly pathetic and very funny.
jokes.explanation: The dark comedy of a grown man maintaining college relationships out of a sense of 'duty' while visiting 'two, three times a week' is quietly devastating. It's a joke that gets funnier the more you think about it — the pride in his own patheticness is very funny.

jokes.text: Broccoli Rob challenge: 'I tell you what. We'll have a sing-off for it. You pick 12 alums from any year to back you up, and I'll do the same. And I'm so confident I'll win, I won't even warm up.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Broccoli Rob are arguing over ownership of 'Faith' as a signature song.
jokes.punchline: Broccoli Rob proposes a formal sing-off with specific rules and then reveals his confidence by announcing he won't warm up — the trash talk of someone who takes a cappella sing-offs very seriously.
jokes.explanation: 'I won't even warm up' is the perfect trash-talk topper for an a cappella rivalry. The specificity of '12 alums from any year' suggests Broccoli Rob has thought about this scenario before — which is its own dark comedy.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Fine, go ahead, thrash your pipes.' / Broccoli Rob: 'My pipes are primo, Champ! Why don't you ask Trey Anastasio about my pipes?'
jokes.setup: Andy sarcastically gives Broccoli Rob permission to warm up.
jokes.punchline: Broccoli Rob invokes Trey Anastasio (of Phish) as a character witness for his vocal quality — the name-drop revealing the absurd a cappella world where this is a legitimate credential.
jokes.explanation: The Trey Anastasio name-drop is a great bit of character specificity — the choice of a jam-band icon as a vocal quality authority is both specific to the Cornell/a cappella world and completely absurd. 'Why don't you ask Trey Anastasio about my pipes?' is a sentence that couldn't exist in any other context.

jokes.text: Broccoli Rob: 'He said, and I quote, "Hey, Rob, nice pipes." That happened!' Andy: 'Okay. Fine, yeah. That's real! That's one guy's opinion. That'll never change!'
jokes.setup: Broccoli Rob has claimed Trey Anastasio complimented his pipes.
jokes.punchline: The actual quote — 'Hey, Rob, nice pipes' — is the blandest possible celebrity endorsement. Andy's furious 'That'll never change!' concedes it happened while stripping it of any significance.
jokes.explanation: The revelation that the Trey Anastasio endorsement is a four-word greeting is perfectly anti-climactic. Andy's acknowledgment — 'That's real! That's one guy's opinion. That'll never change!' — is a masterpiece of someone trying to both concede a point and strip it of meaning simultaneously. The dual frustration of both men about something objectively trivial is great comedy.

jokes.text: Andy calling Broccoli Rob 'Dick' in the middle of the argument
jokes.setup: Andy and Broccoli Rob's argument has reached peak intensity.
jokes.punchline: Andy caps his argument with 'Dick!' — a mild insult deployed with maximum conviction, entirely disproportionate to the stakes of a college a cappella solo dispute.
jokes.explanation: The word 'Dick!' has comic value here mainly from delivery and context — Andy's fury is disproportionate, and the mildness of the insult contrasts with his emotion. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Clark/Kevin: 'I thought that concert was pretty great.' / 'Oh, yeah, I decided acapelco music is awesome.'
jokes.setup: The a cappella concert has just concluded with a furious argument.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's malapropism: 'acapelco music' — a blend of 'a cappella' and 'Acapulco' — delivered with complete confidence, as if this is the correct term.
jokes.explanation: Kevin malapropisms are a reliable show device, but 'acapelco' is a particularly good one — it's plausible as a mishearing, it sounds like a real word, and it implies Kevin has been confidently using this term for a while. The casual delivery ('I decided acapelco music is awesome') suggests he worked himself up to this opinion, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Angela: 'They lost me when they sang Monster Mash. That song obviously glorifies the occult.' Jim: 'Angela, it's Halloween. You have to sing Monster Mash.'
jokes.setup: Angela critiques the concert with her typical humorless moral authority.
jokes.punchline: Monster Mash 'obviously glorifies the occult' — Angela's sincere, paranoid interpretation of a novelty song.
jokes.explanation: A reliable Angela character beat — her interpretation of Monster Mash as occult propaganda is perfectly in character. The setup-punchline is efficient, though the joke relies almost entirely on established character knowledge.

jokes.text: Angela's interrogation of Jim: 'Angela, it's Halloween. You have to sing Monster Mash.' / 'You have to, Jim? You literally have to?' / [Jim falters] / 'Would they go to jail? Would they be shot?'
jokes.setup: Jim uses the casual social 'have to' about singing Monster Mash.
jokes.punchline: Angela takes the 'have to' literally and escalates it into a philosophical interrogation about the nature of obligation — ending at 'Would they be shot?' — systematically destroying Jim's casual assertion.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best exchanges. Angela's forensic deconstruction of 'you have to' — from 'you literally have to?' through 'would they go to jail? Would they be shot?' — is a perfect Angela escalation. It's funny because she's not wrong (Jim IS using 'have to' loosely), but the application of strict logical rigor to Halloween party music is absurd. The escalation to 'be shot' is the ideal stopping point. Jim's deflation ('Okay, we'll just forget it' / 'No, no! I'm interested!') makes it a great two-hander. Angela's character integration is maximal — this exact joke could not be told by anyone else.

jokes.text: Jim's Monster Mash defense: 'Because it is Halloween. So if you're going to sing a concert, it's a good idea to throw that one in.' / Angela: 'Yeah, yeah. No, no, it's a good idea to brush your teeth, but you have to, um, feed your children. Send them to school... all things you can't do if you just keep singing Monster Mash.'
jokes.setup: Jim attempts to defend the casual 'have to' by explaining social norms.
jokes.punchline: Angela's rebuttal escalates to a scenario where someone's inability to stop singing Monster Mash prevents them from feeding their children — a completely unhinged but internally logical argument.
jokes.explanation: The image of someone so compelled to sing Monster Mash that they neglect basic child care is absurd and brilliant. Angela's argument has the structure of genuine logic (good ideas vs. obligations) and collapses it into something genuinely insane. 'All things you can't do if you just keep singing Monster Mash' is among the episode's most quotable lines and a perfect Angela moment — pedantic, humorless, weirdly coherent.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head about the Monster Mash argument: 'It turns out Pam really, really hates Monster Mash. I mean, like, never bring that song up in front of her. Even though Jim was making great points, like, in favor of the song, Pam was like, No! Hate it! Stupid!'
jokes.setup: Jim gives a talking head about the Angela/Monster Mash argument.
jokes.punchline: Jim inexplicably narrates the argument as if Pam was the one objecting, referring to himself in third person ('Jim was making great points') while crediting 'Pam' with Angela's position — either a cover story for the camera or genuine confusion.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly constructed talking-head joke. Jim is apparently protecting Angela (or covering his own embarrassment) by narrating the argument as if Pam were the Monster Mash objector. Referring to himself in third person ('Jim was making great points') is wonderfully odd. The fake Pam impression ('No! Hate it! Stupid!') is a great Jim impression of an Angela impression, and the audience knows the whole thing is a confabulation. This is a sophisticated meta-joke about the documentary format itself — characters managing their image for the camera.

jokes.text: Andy and Russell scene: 'What if we did that? Like, we got jobs, and we were happy all the time?' / 'Oh. Well, Andy, we're not moving to Cornell.'
jokes.setup: Andy laments that his glory days are behind him.
jokes.punchline: Russell has to explicitly tell a grown man 'we're not moving to Cornell' — the fact that Andy had worked himself up to seriously considering this is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between Andy's nostalgic spiral and Russell's patient reality check. 'Like, we got jobs, and we were happy all the time' is a nice encapsulation of misremembered college nostalgia. Andy needing to be explicitly told he can't move back to Cornell is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Duh, I know. That would be insane. Yeah. It could totally work, though. I don't know why we wouldn't.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just agreed that moving to Cornell would be insane.
jokes.punchline: He immediately reverses: 'It could totally work, though. I don't know why we wouldn't.' — the reversal happening within the same breath.
jokes.explanation: The speed of the reversal is the joke. 'Duh, I know. That would be insane.' lasts about one second before Andy's brain catches up with his mouth and he starts reconsidering. 'I don't know why we wouldn't' delivered earnestly after calling it insane is a great Andy character beat — his self-awareness is real but paper-thin.

jokes.text: Andy: 'If I am not Boner Champ... [long pause] ...I don't know who I am.'
jokes.setup: Andy has spiraled into an identity crisis over the Boner Champ dispute.
jokes.punchline: The theatrical pause before 'I don't know who I am' frames a deeply silly problem as an existential crisis.
jokes.explanation: The culminating beat of the Boner Champ arc. The pause is doing enormous work — it signals that Andy is about to say something weighty, and the comedy is that the weight lands on something absurd. 'If I am not Boner Champ... I don't know who I am' is a great line because Andy means it completely, and Ed Helms' delivery makes it emotionally real while the content is ridiculous. A top-five moment in the episode.

jokes.text: Russell resolving Andy's crisis: 'Maybe you're the wise old guy that the new B-O-N-E-R Champ looks up to. You know, you could just... Make a donation.' / 'Well, I was going to say, be a mentor.'
jokes.setup: Russell tries to offer Andy a graceful exit from the Boner Champ identity crisis.
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'I'm going to make a donation' — interpreting 'mentor' as... a financial contribution — reveals a mind that's already moved on from emotional processing to transactional solutions.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from emotional mentorship to a cash donation is a good Andy joke — he's bad at emotional processing but very comfortable with transactional solutions. Russell spelling out 'B-O-N-E-R Champ' is also an odd, funny choice that adds texture.

jokes.text: Russell suggests Andy could be 'the wise old guy that the new Boner Champ looks up to.' / Andy: 'You know, you could just... make a donation.'
jokes.setup: Russell tries to help Andy find a new identity within HCT
jokes.punchline: Andy mishears or misinterprets 'mentor' as 'make a donation' — or deliberately reframes it — then Russell clarifies 'be a mentor' and Andy says 'Yes. I'm going to make a donation.'
jokes.explanation: Andy's pivot from 'wise mentor' to 'I'll just write a check' is a nice character deflation — he'd rather give money than give time, which says something about his emotional availability. The Bernard Family Foundation detail adds texture.

jokes.text: Dwight wanting Nellie's pills: 'Oh, they're not for me. They're for my cousin, Mose. He's just having a tough time, being wifeless, and a high-pressure job, and his crazy cousin Mose.'
jokes.setup: Dwight, having just been told anxiety medication can help, immediately says he wants some.
jokes.punchline: He covers by saying they're 'for my cousin, Mose' — then describes Mose's stressors which are identical to Dwight's own life, culminating in 'his crazy cousin Mose' (i.e., Dwight calling himself crazy).
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The cover story ('for my cousin, Mose') immediately collapses because Dwight accidentally describes his own life. The ultimate self-own is 'his crazy cousin Mose' — Dwight calling himself crazy in the third person while trying to maintain his dignity. It's a perfect callback to the earlier anxiety rant and beautifully resolves Dwight's arc. The structure (deflection → self-description → accidental self-revelation) is impeccable.

jokes.text: 'Other cousin Mose.' / [beat] / 'Got it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just described his cousin Mose's stressor as 'his crazy cousin Mose' — i.e., himself.
jokes.punchline: Dwight adds 'Other cousin Mose' to paper over the slip, and Nellie's flat 'Got it' accepts the fiction with complete diplomatic deadpan.
jokes.explanation: A two-word topper ('Other cousin Mose') that gets maximum comedy from minimum means. 'Other cousin Mose' is simultaneously a desperate cover and an admission — if there's an 'other' Mose, the first Mose is Dwight. Nellie's 'Got it' — equally brief, equally loaded — completes the exchange perfectly. The shared fiction between two people who both know what's really happening is great comedy. Economy: near-perfect.

jokes.text: 'Other cousin Mose. Got it.' — Nellie accepts the Mose/Mose explanation without further comment
jokes.setup: Dwight describes the crazy cousin Mose who is stressing out (the original) Mose
jokes.punchline: Nellie just accepts the existence of two Moses — 'Other cousin Mose. Got it.' — without any pushback, which somehow makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Nellie's flat acceptance is the perfect delivery. Four words of pure deadpan that validate Dwight's entire absurdist construction. Her choice to just... move on... rather than interrogate the obvious paradox is both funny and gracious. Economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: Nellie: 'Well, you tell Mose that he's a good man, and I hope he feels better.' / [beat] / Dwight: 'Which one?' / Nellie: 'Mose, or the real Mose?' / Dwight: 'The real Mose.' / Dwight: 'He says thank you.'
jokes.setup: Nellie plays along with the Mose fiction, sending good wishes to Mose.
jokes.punchline: Dwight can't keep the fiction straight enough to answer 'which Mose?' — the 'real Mose' distinction confirms both that Dwight is Mose and that the cover story has completely collapsed. He then speaks for 'real Mose' with 'he says thank you.'
jokes.explanation: The Mose sequence builds beautifully to this payoff. 'Which one?' is Dwight immediately breaking his own cover. The distinction between 'Mose' and 'the real Mose' (i.e., Dwight himself) is played with complete straight-face sincerity by both characters. 'He says thank you' — Dwight speaking for himself in the third person, accepting Nellie's comfort through a proxy — is deeply funny and weirdly touching. This three-joke sequence (jokes 66-68) is the episode's best sustained comedic writing.

jokes.text: Andy calls his mom about 'a scholarship for a cappella kids at Cornell' to 'wire some money over there' — and she's broke
jokes.setup: Andy, having decided to make a donation as his act of mentorship, calls his mom at the Bernard Family Foundation to arrange it.
jokes.punchline: 'My parents are broke' — the Bernard Family Foundation, which Andy was banking on, turns out to have no money. His fix for his identity crisis collapses immediately.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the Bernard Family Foundation is empty is a good button to Andy's arc — his transactional solution fails because the resources he assumed he had don't exist. The episode seeds the Bernard family financial collapse that becomes a major Season 9 storyline. The a cappella song playing under the reveal gives it a melancholy comedic tone.

jokes.text: Andy calls his mom about wiring money to Cornell for an a cappella scholarship — 'What?' from mom — then: 'My parents are broke.'
jokes.setup: Andy has decided to solve his Boner Champ crisis by funding an HCT scholarship through his family foundation
jokes.punchline: 'My parents are broke' — the Bernard Family Foundation apparently no longer has funds, ending Andy's scheme before it started
jokes.explanation: A solid closing joke for Andy's subplot — his last resort falls through because the Bernard family fortune has apparently collapsed. The flat, defeated delivery of 'My parents are broke' while the a cappella group sings behind him is a nice tonal contrast.

jokes.text: The Cornell alma mater swells over Andy's devastated face as Here Comes Treble sings it — the episode ends with Andy looking at the singing students
jokes.setup: Andy has just learned his parents are broke. His Boner Champ identity is in dispute. His solution failed.
jokes.punchline: The Cornell alma mater played triumphantly over Andy's sad face — the institution Andy has been worshipping all episode delivers a final, unaware gut punch.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed tonal joke — the majestic alma mater scored over Andy's quiet devastation. The comedy comes from the ironic gap between the grandeur of the music and the smallness of Andy's situation. It's funny, a little sad, and very Office. The rewatch value is high because knowing the Bernard financial storyline makes this moment more resonant.

tmdb_overview: It's Halloween in the office and Andy invites his college a cappella group to perform, which leads to a confrontation with his frenemy Broccoli Rob. Meanwhile, Dwight finds evidence that a madman is loose in the office and tries to track him down, and the first meeting of Jim's new job causes a fight with Pam.
